units.title: Skeleton, cartilage, and ligaments
units.summary: Skeleton & Bone Tissue ⚫ The skeleton is composed of bones, joints, cartilage and ligaments ⚫ Joints are the intersections between bones ⚫ Ligaments connects bone at the joints, thus reinforcing the joints Bone Tissue Function ⚫ Support ⚫ Provides significant structural support ⚫ Maintain a posture while accommodating large external forces ⚫ Attachment Sites ⚫ Site of attachment for tendons, muscles and ligaments, thus allows for the generation of movement through the muscular system ⚫ Leverage ⚫ Provides the levers and axes of rotation about which the muscular system generates the movement Cartilage ⚫ 2 main types of cartilages: ⚫ Articular(hyaline) cartilage ⚫ Covers the articulating ends of the bones in the free moving joints ⚫ Function: ⚫ Transit compressive forces across the joint ⚫ Allows motion in the joint with minimal friction ⚫ Redistributes contact stresses over a larger area ⚫ Protects underlying bones ⚫ Fibrocartilage ⚫ Acts as an intermediary between hyaline cartilage and other connective tissues ⚫ Can withstand high pressures ⚫ Refers to as articular disc, or meniscus Ligaments ⚫ Short bands of tough fibrous connective tissue that binds bones to bones ⚫ Provides support in one direction, and often blends with the capsule of the joint ⚫ Capsular ligaments: thickenings in the wall of the capsule ⚫ Extracapsular ligaments: outside the joint ⚫ Intra-articular ligaments: located inside the joint ⚫ Function: ⚫ Guide normal joint movement ⚫ Restrict abnormal joint movement Ligaments: Bone → bone • guides and limits movement

units.title: Joint types
units.summary: Joint – Synovial Joint ⚫ A – articular cartilage ⚫ B + C → joint capsule ⚫ fibrous white connective tissue ⚫ C: synovial membrane ⚫ Secretes synovial fluid into the joint to lubricate & provide nutrition to the joint ⚫ A healthy joint provides effortless motion along preferred anatomical directions with an accompanying restriction of abnormal joint motion Other Types of Joints ⚫ Fibrous Joints ⚫ Little or no movement between the bones & hold the bones together ⚫ Cartilaginous Joints ⚫ Hold bones together with hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage ⚫ The movement is limited Types of Joints in the Human Body (diagram)
summary_sentences: Joint – Synovial Joint ⚫ A – articular cartilage ⚫ B + C → joint capsule ⚫ fibrous white connective tissue ⚫ C: synovial membrane ⚫ Secretes synovial fluid into the joint to lubricate & provide nutrition to the joint ⚫ A healthy joint provides effortless motion along preferred anatomical directions with an accompanying restriction of abnormal joint motion

Other Types of Joints ⚫ Fibrous Joints ⚫ Little or no movement between the bones & hold the bones together ⚫ Cartilaginous Joints ⚫ Hold bones together with hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage ⚫ The movement is limited

units.title: Skeletal muscles and force transmission
units.summary: Functions of Skeletal muscle ⚫ Provide movement ⚫ Muscle actions generate tensions that are transferred to the bone → create skeletal movement ⚫ Maintain Postures and Positions ⚫ Muscle actions of a lesser magnitude ⚫ Muscle activity is continuous ⚫ Stabilize Joints ⚫ Muscle tensions are generated & applied across the joints via tendons, providing stability where they cross the joint Transmission of Muscle force to Bone ⚫ Muscle attaches to bone in 3 ways ⚫ Directly into the bone ⚫ Via a tendon ⚫ Via an aponeurosis

units.title: Muscle roles and actions
units.summary: Insertion ⚫ A muscle typically attaches to a bone at both ends ⚫ Origin: the attachment closest to the middle of the body, or more proximal ⚫ Insertion: the attachment farther from the midline, or more distal; it usually converges to a tendon ⚫ Muscle force is generated & applied to both skeletal connections, resulting in movement of one bone or both Role of Muscle ⚫ Developing Torque ⚫ A muscle controls or creates a movement through the development of torque ⚫ Torque: the tendency of a force (tension) to produce rotation about a specific axis (the joint) ⚫ The amount of tension is influenced by the angle of attachment of the muscle ⚫ Muscle Actions creating, opposing, and stabilizing movements ⚫ In one movement of a joint, e.g. shoulder abduction ⚫ Agonists: muscles creating the movement ⚫ Antagonists: muscles opposing or producing the opposite joint movement ⚫ Stabilizers & Neutralizers: muscles contracting to eliminate the undesired joint action of another muscle Role of Muscle – Shoulder Abduction ⚫ In shoulder abduction, ⚫ Agonist: Deltoid (abductor) ⚫ Abducts the shoulder ⚫ Antagonist: Latissimus dorsi (adductor) ⚫ Resists the abduction ⚫ Stabilizer: Trapezius ⚫ Stabilize and hold the scapula in place ⚫ Neutralizer: Teres minor ⚫ Neutralizes any internal rotation produced by lat. Net Muscle Actions ⚫ Isometric Muscle Action / Contraction ⚫ Muscle tension is generated against resistance to maintain position ⚫ With no visible change in joint position ⚫ Concentric Muscle Action / Contraction ⚫ Muscle visibly shortens while tension is generated ⚫ Eccentric Muscle Action / Contraction ⚫ Muscle lengthens while tension is generated
